entry.title: A telemetry platform on a cluster I ran myself
entry.summary: A CPE monitoring platform built end to end on a self-managed Kubernetes lab, with every shortcut written down and failures rehearsed on purpose.
entry.content:
One post in a series of project retrospectives. Code: huangruidtu/cpemon-mvp

TL;DR: A lab-scale monitoring platform for home routers (CPEs), built end to end on a two-node kubeadm cluster. Simulated devices and a TR-069 server (GenieACS) feed three Go services; MySQL holds the state and doubles as a queue; Prometheus, Grafana, Elasticsearch and Kibana watch it; Velero backs it up. Six decision records explain every shortcut, and the demos break things on purpose and bring them back.

Why build it#

A telemetry platform looks simple from the outside: devices send data, a dashboard shows it. Everything interesting happens in between, and on a large system you usually see only a slice of it.

I wanted the whole loop in my hands, small enough to hold in my head: from a heartbeat leaving a device, through ingress, services, a queue and a database, to a dashboard, a log search, a backup, and a runbook for when it goes wrong. Almost nothing was managed for me. Apart from a container registry and an S3 bucket for backups, everything ran on machines I set up. If something broke, it was mine to find.

The rule I set for the documentation said the same thing from the reader's side: someone with basic Kubernetes knowledge should be able to go from zero to "I can deploy and run this" using only the README, and follow the data the whole way.

The shape of it#

outside the cluster (vm3)      Kubernetes: 1 control plane + 1 worker
-------------------------      --------------------------------------
CPE simulators --heartbeat-->  cpemon-api     --> cpe_status, history
GenieACS ------webhook------>  acs-ingest     --> ingest_events (queue)
                               cpemon-writer  <-- polls the queue

Prometheus + Grafana     metrics from every service
Filebeat + ES + Kibana   logs
Velero + MinIO/S3        namespace backups, MySQL dumps

Three Go services do the work. cpemon-api takes heartbeats and serves the read APIs and a small admin UI. acs-ingest receives webhooks from the ACS. cpemon-writer drains the queue. Everything enters through ingress-nginx, and MetalLB gives the bare-metal cluster a real LoadBalancer IP for it.

The world doesn't start at Kubernetes#

The first real decision was where not to put things. GenieACS and the device simulators run on a separate VM, outside the cluster, and talk to it only through ingress, the way an existing system would.

Putting everything in the cluster would have been tidier. But in telecom, the ACS and the systems around it usually already exist, and a new monitoring layer has to plug into them rather than replace them. The decision record puts it in one line:

I didn't pretend the world starts at Kubernetes.

Six shortcuts, written down#

The lab had two small nodes and one extra VM. That forced shortcuts everywhere, so I wrote each one down as an architecture decision record (ADR): what I chose, what I gave up, and what I'd do at real scale.

Decision What I gave up At real scale
1 control plane + 1 worker, 2 replicas per critical service Surviving a control-plane failure Multiple control-plane nodes, workers across zones
MySQL as the only primary store Separate operational and analytical stores Specialized stores per workload
A queue in MySQL instead of Kafka Partitions, consumer groups, replay Kafka between ingest and processing
Single-node Elasticsearch Log availability A multi-node cluster with lifecycle policies
Plain YAML instead of Helm DRY manifests, multiple environments Helm or Kustomize, plus GitOps
ACS and devices on an external VM A one-command bring-up Keep it: real networks look like this

Every record ends with how the decision would evolve. That turned out to matter: in the later CPEmon upgrade, Kafka replaces the database queue and Helm replaces the plain YAML.

A queue in a database#

The most interesting shortcut is the queue. Kafka would have been the natural choice, but on a two-node lab it would have doubled the moving parts for demo-level traffic. So ACS events go into a MySQL table instead:

  • Idempotent enqueue. A unique key on (sn, event_ts) plus ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE means a webhook delivered twice is stored once.
  • Claiming work. The writer claims an event with a conditional update, status = 'processing' WHERE id = ? AND status = 'queued'. If no row changed, another writer got there first.
  • Retries and dead letters. Each row has attempts, next_at, and a dead state, with exponential backoff from 5 seconds up to 5 minutes and five attempts before giving up.

Webhooks are signed with HMAC-SHA256 and compared in constant time. Every failure path increments a labeled Prometheus counter (invalid_json, missing_sn, invalid_signature), so the dashboard shows why requests fail, not just that they do.

Not all of it was finished. The retry and dead-letter path exists in the schema and code but isn't wired into the writer yet, and heartbeats skip the queue entirely, so the backlog demo (which sends heartbeats) never actually fills it. Signatures are also only checked when a webhook carries the header.

Break it on purpose#

The part I'm happiest with is that failure is part of the demo, not something I hope doesn't happen during it.

  • Drain a node. cpemon-api and acs-ingest run two replicas, spread across both nodes with affinity, tolerations and a PodDisruptionBudget. Draining the worker while a loop polls /healthz shows the API keeps answering.
  • Delete the API. A Velero script backs up the namespace, deletes the cpemon-api Deployment, Service and Ingress, restores them, and runs the smoke test again.
  • Write the runbooks. Three incident runbooks cover a queue backlog, Elasticsearch running out of disk, and a MySQL connection spike, each with impact, likely causes, a diagnostics checklist and immediate actions.

Security got the same layered treatment: the admin UI sits behind Basic Auth and an ingress IP allowlist, and Calico network policies default-deny egress in the namespace, so only the core services can reach MySQL, Prometheus and Elasticsearch.

The admin UI ties it together for an operator: search a device by serial number, see its current state and history, then jump to its metrics in Grafana and its logs in Kibana. A device ID to the evidence in a few clicks.

What it taught me#

Running every layer myself was the fastest way to learn what each layer costs. Elasticsearch needs disk and attention. A database queue works until it doesn't. A single control plane is a single point of failure whatever the replica count says.

It also made the next question obvious: how much of this would I still want to run myself if I didn't have to?

Next#

Next is the same problem with the opposite constraint: no servers at all, only AWS managed services.

entry.title: An edge CI/CD retrospective
entry.summary: My first attempt at treating delivery as one whole problem: layered DevSecOps checks, a self-hosted runner inside a private LAN, versioned artifacts in S3, and a manual rollback.
entry.content:
One post in a series of project retrospectives. Code: huangruidtu/edge-ci-cd-demo

TL;DR: A GitHub Actions pipeline for a C++ app on an ARM board behind a private LAN. Layered checks (cppcheck, Trivy) run on every pull request and fail on high-severity findings. Release tags build a versioned binary on a self-hosted runner, publish it to S3 and deploy it over SSH. Rollback is a manual workflow that redeploys any earlier version from S3.

I started here because this was the first time I treated delivery as a whole problem, rather than as a workflow file that turns green.

The setup#

The application is deliberately trivial: main.cpp prints CI/CD Demo Running!. The less the app does, the more attention goes to the path it takes to production.

The constraints come from the target: an old ARMv7 board running Ubuntu 14.04. It runs a native binary, not containers, and it sits on a private LAN that GitHub's cloud runners can't reach. Almost every decision below follows from those two facts.

I built it in three stages, each answering a concrete problem, instead of writing one big workflow up front.

Day 1: make CI able to fail#

Day one was routine: a C++ skeleton, CMake, a multi-stage Dockerfile, GitHub Actions, a dev / main / PR branching model, and images pushed to ECR.

One small step is worth calling out. The history has these two commits:

Test: break CI intentionally
Fix: restore CI

main.cpp still contains a block, switched off with #if 1, that dereferences a null pointer:

int main() {
    int *p = nullptr;
    *p = 10;   // null pointer dereference
    return 0;
}

I flipped the switch to check that cppcheck actually fails the build. A CI pipeline that has never gone red tells you nothing. Prove it can fail before you trust it when it passes.

The other early decision was tagging. Images started out tagged with the commit SHA; on day two, releases moved to semantic versions such as v1.2.4. The SHA gives traceability; the version gives humans, and later the rollback, something to point at. latest was never used.

Day 2: layer the security checks#

Day two turned CI into a layered DevSecOps pipeline:

Trigger Goal What runs
dev branch Fast feedback cppcheck (SAST) only
PR / main Quality and security gate cppcheck, Docker build, Trivy FS, Trivy image
Tag vX.Y.Z Release and delivery Build a versioned artifact, publish, deploy

Both Trivy scans run with severity: HIGH,CRITICAL and exit-code: 1. They block; they don't just report. A scan that only reports quickly turns into noise nobody reads.

Why not run everything on every branch? On dev it would slow down day-to-day work until people start working around it. Why not only at release? Because problems surface too late. Layering means the checks get stricter the closer code gets to a release.

The same day I added Dependabot. Scanners find risk; Dependabot drives the fix. The policy is simple: merge patches, merge minors and let CI catch problems, test majors by hand. Docker layer caching keeps PR builds from starting from scratch.

Day 3: the hard part of CD isn't in the YAML#

Day three was about getting the binary onto the board. I cut nine tags that day (v1.2.1 to v1.3.1), nearly every one a fix for the previous attempt. Four turning points stand out.

1. Cross-compile first. Install gcc-arm-linux-gnueabihf on a GitHub-hosted runner, build an ARMv7 binary, upload it to S3 by version.

2. Deploy from the build job, then find out it can't reach the board. The first CD step ran scp and ssh straight from the build job. But the board is on a private LAN, and GitHub's cloud runners can't see it. Deployment moved into its own job on a self-hosted runner inside the LAN.

3. New toolchain, old OS. The binary arrived, but binaries from a modern toolchain hit runtime compatibility problems on an OS as old as Ubuntu 14.04. I moved the ARM build to the self-hosted runner as well, and tried lowering the CMake minimum version from 3.10 to 2.8.12. The workflow step is literally named legacy compatibility attempt.

4. Switch off ECR for now. The board consumes a binary, not an image. On this path, pushing to ECR was just noise.

The final pipeline is really two paths:

push / PR / tag --> GitHub-hosted runner
                    cppcheck -> Docker build -> Trivy FS -> Trivy image

tag --------------> self-hosted runner (inside the LAN)
                    build versioned binary -> upload to S3
                    -> download from S3 -> scp to board
                    -> stop.sh / start.sh

The S3 bucket in the middle matters. Every release lands at:

s3://edge-cicd-demo-artifacts/edge-demo/releases/<version>/edge-app

The build only writes there and the deploy only reads from there. Neither side needs to know how the other works, and S3 becomes the source of truth for which versions exist. That is what makes rollback cheap.

Rollback: a separate, manual workflow#

Rollback isn't part of the main pipeline. It's its own workflow_dispatch that takes a version:

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      release_version:
        description: 'Release version to roll back to (e.g. v1.2.4)'
        required: true

It does exactly what a normal deploy does: fetch that version's binary from S3, copy it to the board, and call the board's existing stop.sh / start.sh. Every release is still in S3, so a rollback is just a deploy of an older version. No extra machinery.

Why manual? Rolling back is a sensitive operation. I want it to be explicit: a person decides when, and to which version.

An idea I kept coming back to#

The project never fully solved the board's runtime compatibility. In the docs I recorded it as a separate, platform-specific issue instead of calling the pipeline a failure:

CI/CD orchestration success and target runtime compatibility are not the same problem.

At the time this felt a little like letting myself off the hook. I now think it's an important engineering habit: be clear about what you proved and what you didn't. The orchestration works. The artifact is built, published and delivered to the device. Whether a 2014-era OS can run it is a different question, and collapsing both into "done" or "not done" helps no one.

The habit gets more explicit in later projects. In the platform and data projects I wrote a separate document listing what was actually run and what was only designed or validated offline.

If I did it again#

From the project's own list of next steps:

  • Image signing (Cosign) and an SBOM, so "what is this artifact and where did it come from" can be verified
  • SARIF upload, so scan results land in GitHub Security instead of build logs
  • Progressive delivery instead of an in-place swap

And, looking back:

  • AWS access uses long-lived keys stored in GitHub Secrets. It should use short-lived credentials through GitHub OIDC and STS.
  • Deployment ends as soon as start.sh runs. There's no post-deploy health check, and without one there's no safe automatic rollback.

Next#

Next is the first version of CPEmon: a lab-scale monitoring platform for home routers (CPEs) on a Kubernetes cluster I ran myself. It was my first real look at what "you operate everything" means.
